questions.q: What's the key difference between a Dockerfile's `ENV` and `docker run`'s `-e` flag?
options: ENV is baked into the image at build time, visible to anyone who pulls it; -e is supplied only when a container starts
There is no difference — they behave identically
-e can only be used for numeric values
ENV only works with Python images
questions.explain: ENV becomes part of the image itself; -e exists only for that one running container and is never written to the image.

questions.q: Why is `RUN echo "sk-abc123" > /tmp/key.txt` followed by a later `RUN rm /tmp/key.txt` still a leak risk?
options: RUN instructions cannot create files
The layer from the first RUN is immutable — deleting the file in a later layer hides it, but doesn't remove it from the image's history
rm permanently erases all prior layers automatically
Secrets are automatically encrypted in every layer
questions.explain: A value written during a RUN instruction persists in that layer's history even after a later instruction deletes it — recoverable with `docker history` or by inspecting the layer.

options: Encrypting environment variables automatically
Supplying many environment variables from a file, instead of a long chain of individual -e flags
Baking environment variables into the image permanently
Building an image without any environment variables
questions.explain: --env-file reads variables from a file at container start — the same effect as multiple -e flags, just more manageable, and that file should never be committed to git.

options: It replaces the need for a Dockerfile
It automatically pins all dependency versions
It makes environment variables visible in docker history
It lets a RUN instruction use a secret during the build without that secret being written into any image layer
questions.explain: The secret is available only for the duration of one RUN instruction's filesystem, never committed to a layer — the safe way to use a build-time secret.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where should an OpenAI API key or similar secret go for a running container?
options: Hardcoded directly into the application source code
In a Dockerfile ENV instruction
Supplied at runtime via -e or --env-file, never baked into the image
In a publicly pushed image layer
questions.explain: Secrets should be supplied when the container starts, not baked into the image where anyone who pulls it could see them.
